samples.text:
Nowadays, some governments spend a huge amount of money on space research programmes. There are some advantages and disadvantages of this, which I will explain in this essay.

The first advantage is that space research brings new technology which is useful in our daily life. For example, satellites help us with weather forecast, mobile phones and GPS navigation. Many inventions that was first made for astronauts are now used in hospitals and homes. Secondly, space programmes can make a country proud and they encourage young people to study science and engineering. When children see astronauts on television, they may dream to become scientists in the future. Also, space research help us to understand more about the universe and about our own planet, such as climate change.

On the other hand, the main disadvantage is the cost. Space programmes are extremely expensive, and many people think that this money should be spent on more urgent problems on earth. For instance, in many countries there are still people who do not have enough food, clean water or good hospitals. It seems unfair to spend billions on sending rockets to the space while these people are suffering. Moreover, space missions can be dangerous, and some astronauts have died in accidents. Another problem is that rockets and old satellites create pollution and rubbish in space.

In conclusion, investing in space research has benefits such as new technology and scientific knowledge, but it is also very expensive and some people believe the money should use for poor people. In my opinion, governments should continue space research but spend reasonable amount of money on it.
samples.why: Addresses both advantages and disadvantages · relevant ideas with simple examples, some underdeveloped · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · several agreement, article and verb-pattern errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
A number of governments are committing large budgets to space exploration and research. While these programmes can deliver significant scientific and economic benefits, they are also criticised for their high cost at a time when many problems on Earth remain unsolved.

One of the main advantages of space research is the technology it produces. Satellites, which were developed through space programmes, now support weather forecasting, global communications and navigation systems that people rely on every day. In addition, many innovations originally designed for space missions, such as improved materials and medical equipment, have later found uses in everyday life. Space research also expands scientific knowledge, helping us to understand the origins of the universe and to monitor changes in Earth's climate from above. Furthermore, ambitious space projects can inspire young people to pursue careers in science and engineering, which benefits the wider economy in the long term.

On the other hand, the most common criticism is the enormous expense involved. Critics argue that the money spent on launching rockets could instead be used to improve healthcare, education or housing, or to reduce poverty, which would have a more immediate impact on people's lives. There are also environmental concerns, since rocket launches produce emissions and the growing amount of debris orbiting the planet could damage working satellites. Finally, space missions involve considerable risks, and failures can waste vast sums of money in a matter of seconds.

In conclusion, government investment in space research brings valuable technological progress, scientific understanding and inspiration for future generations. However, its high cost and environmental impact means that governments need to balance this spending carefully against more urgent needs on Earth.
samples.why: Both sides clearly addressed with extended, relevant support · logical organisation and clear paragraph topics · good range of vocabulary (debris, pursue careers) · mostly error-free, one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Space research has long been one of the most expensive and ambitious undertakings a government can pursue, and several countries are now expanding their programmes considerably. The merits of such investment are substantial, but so too are the objections, particularly regarding cost and priorities.

The case in favour rests first on the practical returns. Much of modern life depends on infrastructure that emerged from space programmes: satellites underpin weather forecasting, telecommunications, navigation and disaster monitoring, while technologies developed for spaceflight have been adapted for use in medicine and materials science. Space-based observation is also indispensable for understanding our own planet, providing long-term data on ice cover, sea levels and deforestation that would be impossible to gather from the ground. Beyond these tangible benefits, space exploration pushes the boundaries of human knowledge and, perhaps just as importantly, captures the public imagination, encouraging young people to pursue careers in science and engineering.

Against this, critics raise a powerful moral argument. When public resources are finite, allocating vast sums to exploring distant planets can appear difficult to justify while citizens lack adequate healthcare, housing or education. The benefits of space research are often long-term and uncertain, whereas the needs of the poor are immediate and pressing. There are environmental and practical concerns as well: each launch consumes enormous quantities of fuel, and the accumulation of debris in orbit increasingly threatens the satellites on which everyday services depend. Moreover, national prestige can sometimes drive spending more than genuine scientific value.

In conclusion, government investment in space research yields important technologies, scientific insight and inspiration, yet it competes with urgent social needs and carries environmental risks. The challenge for policymakers is therefore not whether to fund space programmes at all, but how to ensure that such spending remains proportionate and delivers clear public benefit.
samples.why: Sufficiently addresses advantages and disadvantages with well-developed, relevant ideas · logical sequencing and skilful cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (underpin, indispensable, proportionate) · wide range of error-free structures.
